chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Regarding Al-Mudhiha (bone-exposing injury), it is five camels; and regarding Al-Simhaq (injury reaching the bone), it is four camels; and Al-Badhi'a (flesh-exposing injury), it is three camels; and Al-Ma'muma (skull fracture reaching the brain), it is thirty-three camels; and Al-Jaifa (skull injury reaching the inside of the brain), it is thirty-three camels; and Al-Munqila (bone-displacing injury), it is fifteen camels.

key_terms.الْجَائِفَة: Skull injury reaching the inside of the brain

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money for different types of head fractures in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi provides a precise taxonomy of head injuries (such as al-Mudhihah and al-Simhagh) and their corresponding blood money (diyah) in camels, reflecting the early Shia juristic methodology of categorizing damages by depth and extent. It highlights the systematic approach to compensation in Islamic law, where specific terminology distinguishes between superficial fractures and deep brain injuries, ensuring equitable restitution based on the severity of the wound.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al Halby, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said

regarding Al-Mowziha (bone exposing injury) is five from the camels, and regarding Al-Simhak (injury reaching the bone) is four from the camels; and Al-Bazia (flesh exposing injury) is three from the camels; and Al-Mamouma (the skull fracture reaching the brain) is thirty three from the camels; and Al-Jaifa (skull injury reaching the inside of the brain) is thirty three from the camels; and Al-Munqala (bone displacing injury) is fifteen from the camels’.
